Trailwright Kiln 38 pack review

September 2026 · 9 min read

I bought the Kiln 38 in January, straight from Trailwright's online store, for $189. This is the version with the removable lid and the frame that Trailwright calls their "Contour 2.0." I have since carried it on four trips: a weekend in March, a week in June, a three-dayer in August, and a wet nine-miler in September that deserves its own weather report.

What it is

The Kiln 38 is a 38-liter multi-day pack aimed at people who hike their own gear rather than fastpack. Total weight on my kitchen scale was 3 pounds 4 ounces with the lid, 2 pounds 15 without. The frame is a single aluminum hoop with a foam back panel, and the hip belt is the kind that wraps — not the kind that hangs.

What works

The load lifter is the first one I have used that actually pulls the pack onto my back instead of just angling it. A 28-pound load stops feeling like a sack of gravel after about ten minutes, which is a compliment. The hip belt pockets fit a phone and a bar each, and they sit high enough that a pack strap does not grind across them. The front mesh pocket is stretchy in the right direction — taller than it is wide — so a wet shell stays put when you bend over.

The fabric has one honest ding: after eight months the base shows wear where it sits on rocks, but no holes, and the zippers have never caught. Trailwright's warranty is a two-year no-questions deal, and they do honor it; a friend got a replacement buckle in eleven days.

What does not

The removable lid is great, but the frame does not compress when you remove it — the pack just sits there with a floppy collar. The side pockets are tight for two full Nalgene bottles, which is fine for me and annoying for everyone I hike with. And the shoulder straps could use another layer of padding at the base; on a heavy week they started to press.

The verdict

At $189 the Kiln 38 sits between the bargain packs that die in a season and the $350 ultralights that make you handle everything like it is glass. It carries well, weighs a reasonable amount, and the company stands behind it. After eight months and four trips, I think it is worth the extra money.
